anti_patterns: Minting on destination before source finality: a source-chain reorg leaves unbacked tokens with no escrow to slash
Single global minter key with no rate limit or pause: one compromised key yields infinite unbacked supply on every chain
Granting minter roles to unverified bridge adapters: any authorized caller can inflate supply (ERC-7802 warns against this explicitly)
Using burn-mint for wrapped representations of single-home assets (e.g. WETH): minting without control of the underlying collateral creates uncollateralized tokens
Skipping remote-pool whitelisting: destination accepts mint messages from arbitrary source contracts (replay/forgery)
Ignoring decimal and selector mismatches across chains: silent amount distortion when token variants differ
avoid_when: The asset has a single home chain and only needs representation elsewhere (lock-and-mint with one escrow is simpler)
The token contract is non-upgradeable and cannot grant minter roles (requires a lockbox migration first)
Sub-second cross-chain latency is required (destination mint must wait source finality)
No trustworthy attestation layer exists between the chains (mint authority cannot be safely delegated)
Only one chain is involved (no cross-chain movement at all)
benefits: No escrow honeypot: nothing is locked on the source chain, so there is no central pool of collateral to steal (unlike lock-and-mint bridges)
Canonical fungibility: the token on every chain is the native asset, not a bridge-specific wrapped IOU, so liquidity is never fragmented across wrapped variants
Capital efficiency: destination chains need no pre-seeded liquidity since tokens are minted on demand against proven burns
Constant global supply by construction: every mint is preceded by an equal burn, so sum of supply across chains is invariant
Standardized token interface: ERC-7802 crosschainMint/crosschainBurn give every bridge the same two entry points instead of per-bridge mint/burn dialects
Independent per-chain rate limiting and pausing: each deployment bounds inbound/outbound flow without coordinating a shared escrow
best_practices: Separate crosschain mint/burn functions from local mint/burn (ERC-7802): access-control or limit changes never touch the base token logic
Gate minter/burner roles behind multisig or governance timelock; never a single EOA in production
Configure per-lane inbound/outbound rate limiters (capacity + refill rate) on every pool and test the pause path
Whitelist remote pool addresses bilaterally on every chain before enabling a lane; include old pool addresses during migrations so in-flight messages validate
Emit and index CrosschainMint/CrosschainBurn events (plus ERC-20 Transfer to/from zero address) for supply auditing
Verify ERC-165 interface support (0x33331994) locally on each chain before granting roles; cross-chain consistency is the bridge's job
Plan minter-role revocation propagation: removing a chain must revoke its adapter's roles on all remaining deployments
component_types: Burn/Mint Token Contract: ERC-20 (or SPL) asset exposing permissioned crosschainMint/crosschainBurn entry points (ERC-7802 interface)
Bridge Adapter / Token Pool: per-chain contract holding MINTER/BURNER roles; executes burn on send, verifies attestation and mints on receive (e.g. CCIP BurnMintTokenPool, LayerZero OFT)
Attestation / Messaging Network: oracle, DVN set, or light-client network that observes source finality and delivers the burn proof to the destination
Rate Limiter: per-lane inbound/outbound flow caps (capacity plus refill) bounding mint blast radius
Nonce / Replay Registry: per-message identifiers guaranteeing each burn authorizes exactly one mint
Supply Monitor / Indexer: off-chain agent tracking CrosschainMint/CrosschainBurn events to audit the global supply invariant
context: A natively multi-chain token (stablecoin, governance, or utility token deployed on several chains) must move between chains while staying the same canonical asset everywhere. Lock-and-mint bridging fragments liquidity into per-bridge wrapped variants and concentrates locked collateral into theft-prone escrows. The burn-mint bridge instead destroys tokens on the source chain and reissues the identical amount on the destination chain after attestation, keeping total cross-chain supply constant with no escrow and no wrapped tokens.
design_principles: Supply Conservation: every destination mint must be causally preceded by an equal source burn; global circulating supply never changes
Burn Before Mint: the burn transaction must reach finality on the source chain before any mint is authorized
Least-Privilege Mint Authority: only explicitly authorized bridge adapters hold minter/burner roles, scoped per chain and revocable
Explicit Attestation: no mint executes on an unverified claim; a configured attestation network must confirm the burn
Fail Closed: on attestation doubt, timeout, or rate-limit breach, the transfer halts rather than minting optimistically
Local Interface Consistency: each deployment independently verifies ERC-7802 support; the bridge guarantees cross-chain consistency
name: burn-mint-bridge
references: skeletor, parti, joxes et al., ERC-7802: Token With Mint/Burn Access Across Chains, 2024 — https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7802

technology_stack: EVM chains + Solana SPL (Pool Signer PDA)
tradeoffs: Minter-key compromise is catastrophic: whoever holds the minter role can inflate supply on every chain, so key management and role governance dominate operational cost
Latency bound by source finality: destination mint waits for the burn to finalize (15-20 minutes on Ethereum L1/L2s), which rules out instant transfers without additional fast-finality layers
Two transactions plus attestation fees: every transfer pays source burn gas, messaging/verification fees, and destination mint gas
Liveness depends on the attestation network: stalled or censored relayers/oracles freeze transfers even though both chains are healthy

Cross-chain heterogeneity burden: decimals, function selectors, address formats, and finality rules must be normalized per lane (LayerZero exposes configurable burn/mint selectors for exactly this reason)
Chain onboarding is N-way work: each new chain requires minter-role grants and bilateral remote-pool configuration on all existing deployments
use_cases: Multi-chain stablecoin transfers preserving one canonical fungible asset on every chain (e.g. CCTP-style USDC movement)
Governance token mobility: voting power moves natively between chains without wrapped IOUs
Standardizing per-bridge mint/burn dialects behind one ERC-7802 token interface
Migrating a lock-and-mint bridged token to escrow-free native transfers to remove honeypot risk
Real-world-asset tokens requiring auditable constant-supply movement across networks
